clinicalPearls: The rarest of the mucopolysaccharidoses, caused by deficiency of lysosomal hyaluronidase (HYAL1), leading to accumulation of hyaluronan rather than the sulfated glycosaminoglycans that accumulate in the other MPS subtypes.
The hallmark is nodular periarticular soft-tissue masses around large joints, which may wax and wane with episodes of painful swelling.
Unlike Hurler, Hunter and most other MPS types, cognition and neurodevelopment are characteristically preserved, and there is typically no corneal clouding or coarse facies.
Mild short stature and only subtle facial changes may occur; visceromegaly is characteristically absent.
Because standard urinary screening detects sulfated glycosaminoglycans, conventional MPS urine screens can be normal, which is a major diagnostic pitfall.
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating deficient hyaluronidase activity together with raised circulating hyaluronan, confirmed by HYAL1 molecular testing.
Excised nodules show storage-laden histiocytes and macrophages, and lesions may be mistaken for tumour or inflammatory arthritis.
No specific enzyme replacement therapy is available; care is supportive and multidisciplinary.
reference.pathophysiology: Mucopolysaccharidosis type IX is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in HYAL1 on chromosome 3p21.3, which encodes lysosomal hyaluronidase 1. Deficient enzyme activity impairs degradation of hyaluronan (hyaluronic acid), a large non-sulfated glycosaminoglycan of the extracellular matrix, causing its accumulation within lysosomes and periarticular connective tissue. The resulting histiocytic and macrophage storage produces nodular soft-tissue masses, predominantly around large joints, with relatively little visceral, skeletal or neurological involvement. Crucially, because hyaluronan is not sulfated, it escapes detection by the conventional urinary glycosaminoglycan electrophoresis used to screen for other MPS subtypes, explaining why routine screening may appear falsely normal.
additionalDifferentials: Other lysosomal storage disorders with soft-tissue deposits
additionalInvestigations: Leukocyte or fibroblast hyaluronidase enzyme assay
Ultrasound and MRI of periarticular masses
Histology of an excised nodule looking for storage-laden histiocytes
Urinary glycosaminoglycan analysis to exclude other MPS subtypes
Skeletal survey to assess acetabular and periarticular changes
redFlags: Recurrent painful periarticular swellings misinterpreted as an inflammatory arthropathy
A normal urinary glycosaminoglycan screen giving false reassurance
Soft-tissue masses prompting biopsy under suspicion of malignancy
Short stature accompanied by preserved cognition and no coarse facies
reference.prognosis: Generally a mild mucopolysaccharidosis with preserved cognition and a near-normal lifespan, morbidity arising mainly from recurrent periarticular masses and joint symptoms. Because so few cases have been described, long-term outcome data remain limited.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal urinary glycosaminoglycan screen excludes an MPS
Misdiagnosing periarticular masses as neoplasm or juvenile idiopathic arthritis
Overlooking the diagnosis because it is exceptionally rare
Expecting corneal clouding, coarse facies or organomegaly, which are usually absent
management: Management is supportive, as no enzyme replacement therapy is available for hyaluronidase deficiency
Treat painful periarticular soft-tissue masses with analgesia and anti-inflammatory agents, and surgically excise symptomatic or disabling nodules
Provide physiotherapy and joint-directed care for the recurrent painful swelling around large joints
Monitor for recurrence of periarticular masses after excision
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder with family testing
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across clinical genetics, rheumatology and orthopaedics
